List Update with Time Windows and Delays without Batch-Serving

Research partly supported by NSF grant CCF-2218677, ONR grant ONR-13533312, and the Wai T. Chang Chair in Industrial Engineering and Operations Research.Authors emails: icey.ai@columbia.edu, jl6639@columbia.edu, and cliff@ieor.columbia.edu.
Icey Siyi Ai Affiliation: Department of Industrial Engineering and Operations Research, Columbia University.    Jingwei Li Affiliation: Department of Industrial Engineering and Operations Research, Columbia University.    Clifford Stein Affiliation: Department of Industrial Engineering and Operations Research, Columbia University.
Abstract

We study list update with time windows and delays when every request requires a separate access. Unlike batch-serving models, serving several requests to one element still incurs one access per request, and each access may change the list for subsequent requests. For time windows of overlap at most k≥2k\geq 2, our deterministic First-Element Removal algorithm is (3−2/k)(3-2/k)-competitive, hence 33-competitive in general. Against an oblivious adversary, a randomized adaptation of BIT is 7/47/4-competitive on arbitrary 22-overlap inputs. More generally, on inputs without self-overlap, it is (13/4−9/[2​(k+1)])\left(13/4-9/[2(k+1)]\right)-competitive for every k≥2k\geq 2. For delays, we give a deterministic 55-competitive algorithm and a lower bound of 2+32+\sqrt{3} for deterministic delay-unaware algorithms. Our analyses extend inversion potentials with per-request credits that reconcile different service times and orders.

1 Introduction

The list update problem is a fundamental problem in online algorithms and competitive analysis. First studied by McCabe [22] as a model for maintaining a sequential file, it was later used by Sleator and Tarjan [27] to introduce competitive analysis. In the classical list update problem, requests for elements in a list arrive online and must be accessed and served immediately. Serving an element costs its current position in the list; immediately after the access, the algorithm may move the accessed element forward for free, and it may also swap two adjacent elements at a cost of 1 at any time. The objective is to minimize the total access and paid-swap cost.

Many online settings relax the requirement that requests must be served immediately upon arrival. Two common relaxations are time windows, where a request may be served any time between its release time and deadline, and delays, where a request may be served later at the cost of accumulating a delay penalty. Such relaxations have been studied for various online problems, including paging (caching)[17], multilevel aggregation[21, 13], and set cover[6]. They capture situations in which an online algorithm can wait in order to reorder, batch, or otherwise coordinate its actions.

In recent work, Azar et al. [8] introduced time window and delay models for the list update problem. A distinctive feature of their model is a batch-serving rule: a single access may serve any set of alive requests, at a cost equal to the position of the furthest element in the set. This rule is powerful and natural in settings where one action can satisfy many pending requests, but it can be too strong when requests represent distinct operations that must each be executed. For example, consider an adaptive data service that keeps records or cached objects in a priority list. The position of an object represents the cost of locating or loading it, and accessing the object may justify promoting it in the list. Each request, however, is a separate transaction on a specified object, possibly with its own user, input, validation, or update. Thus, even if several requests are handled in the same time step, each request incurs its own access cost.

Motivated by such applications, in this paper we study the list update problem with time windows and delays, without batch serving: each request must still be paid for separately, even if several requests are served at the same time. Because each access may trigger a free forward move that reconfigures the list, the order in which simultaneous or overlapping requests are served becomes part of the algorithmic decision. We call this the No-Batching-Allowed list update model with time windows or delays, or NBA list update for short. It captures settings where each request is a distinct unit of work, so that serving one request does not automatically serve the others. The resulting model is incomparable with the batch-serving model of Azar et al.[8]: both generalize the classical list update problem in [22], but neither contains the other. As we will see below, our competitive ratios are significantly smaller than those in [8], but a direct comparison is not particularly informative.

Removing batch-serving introduces a new difficulty when time windows overlap: the algorithm must choose an order in which to serve pending requests, and each access may rearrange the list for the remaining requests. We capture this with an overlap parameter kk: an instance is kk-overlap if at most kk time windows contain any given time tt, including time windows of requests for the same list item. When k=1k=1, the problem reduces to the classical setting. This parameter has a natural operational interpretation as a bound on simultaneous demand, such as the number of open sessions, active users, queued transactions, or pending tasks a system may have at once. Small kk corresponds to lightly loaded or tightly scheduled systems, while large kk captures higher congestion. Besides bounds for general inputs, we obtain refined guarantees in terms of the maximum overlap. For example, our deterministic algorithm FER is 3-competitive under general inputs, but also (3−2/k)(3-2/k)-competitive for kk-overlap, interpolating between the general guarantee of 33 and the competitive lower bound 22 at k=2k=2, achieving optimum under the latter case.

Azar et al. [8] leave open whether randomization can improve their deterministic bounds for the batch-serving models. We obtain such improvements in our non-batch time-window model on inputs without self-overlap, meaning that the time windows of requests to the same element are disjoint. This condition has a natural operational interpretation in systems where clients interact sequentially with a shared server. Each list element may store information associated with one client, who waits for a response before submitting the next operation. When responses are returned at the requests’ deadlines, successive requests from that same client have disjoint windows, although requests from different clients may overlap. On kk-overlap inputs without self-overlap, our randomized algorithm WBIT achieves competitive ratio 13/4−9/[2​(k+1)]13/4-9/[2(k+1)] for every k≥2k\geq 2, improving FER’s guarantee for 2≤k≤72\leq k\leq 7 and matching it at k=8k=8. (FER and WBIT are defined below.) For k=2k=2, we can remove the no-self-overlap restriction and obtain a 7/47/4-competitive guarantee, separating the deterministic and randomized regimes by breaking the deterministic lower bound of 22 in this setting.

1.1 Our results

Our results are summarized in Table 1.

The new models. We formulate No-Batching-Allowed list update with time windows and delays. Each request requires a separate access and every access allows moving the accessed element forward for free. Consequently, serving one request can change the list and the cost of serving the remaining requests, so the algorithm must choose both when and in what order to serve them. In contrast, the batch-serving models of Azar et al. [8] allow one access to serve several pending requests at once but charge for all swaps. See further related work in Section 1.2.

For the batch-serving models, Azar et al. [8] give competitive ratios of 2424 for time windows and 336336 for delays using deterministic algorithms without advance knowledge of deadlines or future delay costs. These results motivate us to study the role of randomization and advance information in our non-batch models.

Deterministic algorithms for time windows. Our main deterministic algorithm, First-Element Removal (FER), combines the classical move-to-front (MTF)11 1 In classical list update, the move-to-front (MTF) algorithm serves each request immediately and then moves the accessed element to the front for free. MTF is 22-competitive [27], matching the lower bound of 22 for deterministic online algorithms uniformly over all list sizes [24]. with a simple rule for early service. Choosing this rule is crucial: serving every request upon arrival, at its deadline, or after clearing all cheaper pending requests as in batch-serving can each lead to a competitive ratio of Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n) (Section 3.1). FER only serves requests to the element at the head of its list early, yet achieves a competitive ratio of 3−2k3-\frac{2}{k} on kk-overlap inputs for k≥2k\geq 2 (Section 3.2).

Randomized algorithms for time windows. Our randomized algorithm WBIT serves requests at deadlines and uses the classical BIT22 2 BIT assigns each element an independent uniformly random initial bit. It serves each request immediately, moves the accessed element to the front if its bit is 00, and then flips the bit in either case. BIT is 7/47/4-competitive against an oblivious adversary [24]. rule [24] to decide whether to move the accessed element to the front. For every k≥2k\geq 2, WBIT is (134−92​(k+1))\left(\frac{13}{4}-\frac{9}{2(k+1)}\right)-competitive on kk-overlap inputs without self-overlap (Section 4). This improves FER’s guarantee for 2≤k≤72\leq k\leq 7 and matches it at k=8k=8. For k=2k=2, we remove the no-self-overlap restriction and obtain a ratio of 7/47/4 on all 22-overlap inputs, strictly below the deterministic lower bound of 22.

Algorithm and lower bound for delays. We distinguish the delay-aware regime, in which each request’s delay function is known upon arrival, from the delay-unaware regime, in which only incurred delay costs are observed. Our Delayed Move-to-Front algorithm (DMF) uses accumulated delay relative to access cost to determine when to access an element and move it to the front, achieving a competitive ratio of 55 in both regimes (Section 5). We also prove a lower bound of 2+3≈3.7322+\sqrt{3}\approx 3.732 for every deterministic delay-unaware algorithm, separating this setting from classical list update, whose optimal deterministic ratio is 22.

Technical contributions. The challenge in analyzing list update with time windows is that OPT and the online algorithm may serve requests at different times. To address this challenge we need to go beyond the standard inversion counting potential functions. For each request served first by OPT, the potential retains part of OPT’s access cost and maintains request-specific accounts that track subsequent changes in the two lists. The overlap bound limits how many such accounts a service can affect. For WBIT, these accounts are combined with BIT’s bit-weighted inversions [24]; for delays, they are applied to groups of requests served consecutively by DMF.

We also take advantage of the time windows and delays by allowing some request-specific terms in the potential function to be negative until they are served by both OPT and ALG. Once all requests have been served, however, the potential is nonnegative, which is sufficient for the amortized analysis.

Our time-window lower bounds use two constructions. For hh-local-lazy MTF algorithms, requests are released only after their elements have moved beyond the first hh positions, preventing early service. For the tighter FER lower bound, the fixed request order e1,…,ene_{1},\ldots,e_{n} is repeated arbitrarily many times. Repeating this pattern for a fixed list size makes the additive constant negligible. In contrast, the delay lower bound chooses requests adaptively based on the online algorithm’s actions, exploiting delay-unawareness.

1.2 Related work

Classical algorithms and bounds.

The survey by Kamali and López-Ortiz [19] provides a comprehensive overview of list-update algorithms and models. Besides MTF, deterministic 22-competitive algorithms include TIMESTAMP [3] and the Move-to-Recent-Item (MRI) family [16]. For randomized algorithms against an oblivious adversary, the COUNTER family generalizes BIT and gives competitive ratios arbitrarily close to 3\sqrt{3} [24]. COMB combines BIT and TIMESTAMP and is 8/58/5-competitive [2], while Teia [28] proved a randomized lower bound of 3/23/2. Further algorithmic results appear in [26, 18, 25].

Alternative cost models.

Variants of list update include the paid-exchange model, in which all exchanges are paid [1], the partial-cost model [3, 4], and the uniform-cost model [10]. In the partial-cost model, accessing the element at position jj costs j−1j-1, rather than jj. For this model, Ambühl et al. [4] proved a randomized lower bound of approximately 1.500841.50084. Recent work also studies list update under i.i.d. requests, including near-optimal expected access costs for the Transposition rule [14, 23].

Other problems with time windows and delays.

Time-window and delay models have also been studied in paging and caching [7, 17], multilevel aggregation [21, 13], set cover [6], matching [12, 5, 20, 15], and facility location [11]. Azar and Touitou [9] developed a general framework for online metric optimization problems with deadlines or delay costs.

2 Preliminaries

2.1 List update with time windows

We are given a list LL of nn distinct elements in a specific initial order. The input is a sequence of mm requests σ={σi}i∈[m]\sigma=\{\sigma_{i}\}_{i\in[m]}. Each request has the form σi=(ei,ri,di)\sigma_{i}=(e_{i},r_{i},d_{i}), consisting of a requested element ei∈Le_{i}\in L, a release time rir_{i}, and a deadline di≥rid_{i}\geq r_{i}. We index requests in nondecreasing order of their release times. The input is online: request σi\sigma_{i} is revealed only at time rir_{i}.

To serve request σi\sigma_{i}, an algorithm ALG must access element eie_{i} at some time in the interval [ri,di][r_{i},d_{i}]. Every request requires a separate access, including requests to the same element. We use the full cost model of Sleator and Tarjan [27]: accessing the jj-th element ee of the list costs jj; immediately afterward, ALG may move ee forward to any position in the list for free. Any adjacent swaps by ALG are allowed at any time with a cost of 1. The objective is to minimize the total access and paid-swap cost. We write ALG​(σ)\textsc{ALG}{}(\sigma) for the cost of algorithm ALG on input σ\sigma, and OPT​(σ)\textnormal{{OPT}}{}(\sigma) for the optimal offline cost.

We work in integral time. At every time step, all releases are processed before any service actions. Multiple actions may then occur at the same time, but their order must be specified. In particular, each access is immediately followed by its free move before the next action. Thus, when several requests have the same deadline, an algorithm may choose their service order, and each service may change the list before the next request is served.

The window of request σi\sigma_{i} contains time tt if ri≤t≤dir_{i}\leq t\leq d_{i}. This is a property of the input. For a particular algorithm, σi\sigma_{i} is alive at time tt if its window contains tt and the algorithm has not yet served it. We use the parameter k≥1k\geq 1 to denote the maximum overlap number among the time windows of requests. An input is kk-overlap if, for every time tt, the windows of at most kk requests contain tt. We say that an input has no self-overlap if the time windows of any two distinct requests to the same element are disjoint; otherwise, it has self-overlap.

The classical list update problem is the special case of this model where every request has a distinct point window, ri=dir_{i}=d_{i}. Thus the time-window model inherits the classical lower bounds, including the deterministic lower bound of 22 and the randomized lower bound of 1.51.5 against an oblivious adversary.

2.2 List update with delays

In the delay model, a request σi\sigma_{i} specifies an element eie_{i}, a release time rir_{i}, and a delay function fi​(t)f_{i}(t) for t≥rit\geq r_{i}. If the request is served at time tt, the algorithm pays fi​(t)f_{i}(t) in addition to the access and paid-swap costs. As in the time-window model, every request requires a separate access.

Time in the delay model is continuous. Releases, accesses, and swaps may occur at arbitrary nonnegative real times, and accesses and swaps are instantaneous. At a common time, all releases occur before service actions, and each schedule specifies the order of its accesses and moves.

A request is pending if it has been released but has not yet been served. A delay-aware algorithm learns fif_{i} when σi\sigma_{i} is released. A delay-unaware algorithm continuously observes the current delay of every pending request but does not know future delay values. Further assumptions on the delay functions are given in Section 5.

The delay model also contains classical list update as a special case: delay functions can make postponing a request until the next release extremely expensive. Hence the classical list-update lower bounds apply here as well.

2.3 Notation

For an algorithm ALG, let posALGt​(e)\mathrm{pos}^{t}_{\textsc{ALG}}(e) be the position of element ee in ALG’s list at time tt; we omit tt or ALG when clear. We write a≺ALGba\prec_{\textsc{ALG}}b if aa precedes bb in the current list maintained by ALG. A request σi\sigma_{i} is pre-served for an online algorithm ALG at time tt if OPT has served σi\sigma_{i} by time tt but ALG has not. We write tiOPTt_{i}^{\textnormal{{OPT}}{}} and tiALGt_{i}^{\textsc{ALG}{}} for the times at which OPT and ALG serve σi\sigma_{i}, respectively, and call the interval [tiOPT,tiALG)[t_{i}^{\textnormal{{OPT}}{}},t_{i}^{\textsc{ALG}{}}) the pre-service interval of σi\sigma_{i}. We write yiy_{i} for the position of eie_{i} in OPT’s list at time tiOPTt_{i}^{\textnormal{{OPT}}{}}, and xix_{i} for the position of eie_{i} in ALG’s list at time tiALGt_{i}^{\textsc{ALG}{}}.

We analyze our algorithms using a different potential function Φ\Phi for each algorithm. To prove a competitive ratio of cc, we establish Δ​ALG+Δ​Φ≤c⋅Δ​OPT\Delta\textsc{ALG}{}+\Delta\Phi\leq c\cdot\Delta\textnormal{{OPT}}{} for every event, taking expectations in the randomized case.

3 Deterministic Algorithms for Time Windows

Our deterministic algorithm builds on the classic move-to-front rule. However, we must also decide when and in what order to serve requests. We first show that several natural choices lead to competitive ratios of Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n).

3.1 Limits of simple serving orders

Lemma 3.1.

In the time-window model for list update, each of the following deterministic serving rules has competitive ratio Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n), where nn is the list length:

  1. (a)

    serving every request consistently in either arrival order or deadline order;

  2. (b)

    waiting until the next deadline did_{i}, then serving all alive requests whose elements precede eie_{i} in the current list, followed by σi\sigma_{i}.

See Appendix A.1 for proofs. These examples show that a good algorithm can rely neither on timing alone nor on greedily serving all currently cheap requests; it must balance patience against a selective use of list positions.

3.2 First-Element Removal and its bounded-overlap analysis

First-Element Removal (FER) is given in Algorithm 1. It acts only at deadlines; before serving the expiring request, it clears alive requests for the element currently at the head of the list. We call this the head-clearance step. Each such access costs 11 and leaves the list unchanged. It then serves the expiring request and moves its element to the front.

All actions at a deadline are instantaneous and executed in the stated order, as described in Section 2. Thus head-clearance does not cause deadline violations. If several deadlines occur at the same time, FER processes the corresponding requests in a fixed order.

We now upper-bound FER in terms of the input’s overlap number kk.

Theorem 3.2.

For every k≥2k\geq 2 and every kk-overlap input σ\sigma,

FER​(σ)≤(3−2k)​OPT​(σ).\textnormal{{FER}}(\sigma)\;\leq\;\Bigl(3-\frac{2}{k}\Bigr)\,\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma).

3.2.1 Reductions for the analysis of FER

Throughout the proof of Theorem 3.2 we make the following standing assumptions, without loss of generality:

  • (A1)

    the input is kk-overlap for some k≥2k\geq 2 and has no self-overlap;

  • (A2)

    OPT uses no free exchanges;

  • (A3)

    FER serves no requests in its head-clearance steps. As a result, every FER action is a deadline access followed by a move to the front.

The next two lemmas justify (A1)–(A3). Lemma 3.3 justifies (A2) without changing the input; Lemma 3.4 deletes requests to obtain an input satisfying (A1) and (A3) with no decrease in the cost ratio FER/OPT\textnormal{{FER}}/\textnormal{{OPT}}. Both reductions preserve the kk-overlap property.

Lemma 3.3.

For any input σ\sigma there exists an optimal schedule that uses no free exchanges.

Proof.

Take an optimal schedule. Suppose it uses free exchange: it serves a request to element xx at time tt by accessing xx at position pp and then moves xx forward ii positions for free. Replace this action by first moving xx forward using ii paid exchanges, then accessing it at position p−ip-i, with both steps performed at time tt. The replacement costs i+(p−i)=pi+(p-i)=p and leaves the list in the same order, preserving feasibility and all subsequent actions. Repeating this replacement eliminates all free exchanges while preserving optimality. ∎

For the following reduction, we assume that requests released at time tt are available before FER takes action at tt. Fix an order for simultaneous deadlines and retain this order when requests are deleted.

Lemma 3.4.

Let σ\sigma be a nonempty input. Simulate FER on σ\sigma. Whenever FER processes an unserved request σk\sigma_{k} at its deadline, mark for deletion all other alive requests whose element is either eke_{k} or the current head. Let σ′\sigma^{\prime} consist of the unmarked requests.

Then σ′\sigma^{\prime} has no self-overlap, FER never serves a request through head clearance on σ′\sigma^{\prime}, and

FER​(σ)OPT​(σ)≤FER​(σ′)OPT​(σ′).\frac{\textnormal{{FER}}(\sigma)}{\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma)}\leq\frac{\textnormal{{FER}}(\sigma^{\prime})}{\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma^{\prime})}.
Proof.

Let m′m^{\prime} be the number of marked requests for deletion. We first compare FER’s executions on σ\sigma and σ′\sigma^{\prime}.

Every marked request is served at cost 11 without changing the list. A request marked because its element is currently at the head is served immediately during head clearance. Otherwise, it is a request to the element eke_{k} of the current request σk\sigma_{k}. After serving σk\sigma_{k}, FER moves eke_{k} to the front. At the next deadline at which FER acts, the marked request is either served during head clearance or is itself the expiring request. In either case, it is served while eke_{k} is still at the front.

We must also account for deadlines that disappear when marked requests are deleted. If a marked request is itself the expiring request that causes FER to act, every request served during head clearance at that time is also marked. Thus removing that deadline removes only services of marked requests.

An induction over the original execution now shows that FER serves the surviving requests in the same order and from the same list positions on σ′\sigma^{\prime} as on σ\sigma. Consequently, FER​(σ)=FER​(σ′)+m′.\textnormal{{FER}}(\sigma)=\textnormal{{FER}}(\sigma^{\prime})+m^{\prime}.

By Lemma 3.3, choose an optimal schedule for σ\sigma with no free exchanges. Delete its accesses to the marked requests while retaining all paid exchanges. This preserves the list evolution and gives a feasible schedule for σ′\sigma^{\prime}, saving at least one unit per deleted request. Hence OPT​(σ)≥OPT​(σ′)+m′.\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma)\geq\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma^{\prime})+m^{\prime}.

The first deadline trigger survives, so σ′\sigma^{\prime} is nonempty. Since FER​(σ′)≥OPT​(σ′)>0\textnormal{{FER}}(\sigma^{\prime})\geq\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma^{\prime})>0,

FER​(σ)OPT​(σ)≤FER​(σ′)+m′OPT​(σ′)+m′≤FER​(σ′)OPT​(σ′).\frac{\textnormal{{FER}}(\sigma)}{\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma)}\leq\frac{\textnormal{{FER}}(\sigma^{\prime})+m^{\prime}}{\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma^{\prime})+m^{\prime}}\leq\frac{\textnormal{{FER}}(\sigma^{\prime})}{\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma^{\prime})}.

We finally verify that σ′\sigma^{\prime} has no self-overlap. Suppose two surviving requests to the same element have intersecting windows. At the start of the earlier of their deadline steps, the other request has arrived and is still unserved. It would therefore be marked, a contradiction. We also check that in σ′\sigma^{\prime}, every head-clearance request in the original execution was marked. Thus FER serves every surviving request in σ′\sigma^{\prime} in its own deadline step, with no head-clearance accesses. ∎

Lemma 3.5.

Remark 3.8.

Theorem 3.2 implies that FER is 33-competitive for unrestricted inputs. For k=2k=2, it is 22-competitive, matching the deterministic lower bound inherited from classical list update.

3.3 Lower bound for FER and local lazy MTF rules

First we give a lower bound for a natural, broader class of MTF-based algorithms.

Definition 3.9 (hh-local-lazy MTF).

Let h∈{0,1,…,n−1}h\in\{0,1,\ldots,n-1\}. A deterministic online algorithm is hh-local-lazy MTF if it (i) uses no paid exchanges, (ii) moves every accessed element to the front, and (iii) serves a request before its deadline only when its element is in one of the first hh positions.

The definition permits, but does not require, early service in the first hh positions. MTF at deadlines is hh-local-lazy for every hh, and FER is hh-local-lazy for every h≥1h\geq 1.

Theorem 3.10.

Fix integers n≥3n\geq 3 and 1≤h<n/21\leq h<n/2. Every deterministic hh-local-lazy MTF algorithm AA admits an input σ\sigma without self-overlap such that

A⁡(σ)OPT​(σ)≥n2​n​(n−h)−n+h+1.\frac{A(\sigma)}{\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma)}\geq\frac{n}{\sqrt{2n(n-h)}-n+h+1}.

The construction and offline schedule appear in Appendix A.2. When h=o⁡(n)h=o(n), it tends to 1+21+\sqrt{2}. This theorem is a lower bound on worst-case cost ratios. We further show that our 3-competitive analysis is tight. The proof is deferred to Appendix A.3.

Theorem 3.11.

The competitive ratio of FER is 33.

4 Randomized Algorithms for Time Windows

We adapt the classical BIT algorithm to time windows. WBIT serves every request at its deadline and applies BIT’s randomized move rule (Algorithm 2). It initially chooses independent uniform bits and fixes any ordering of simultaneous deadlines independently of them. Against an oblivious adversary, WBIT is 7/47/4-competitive on all 22-overlap inputs, matching classical BIT’s guarantee [24] and beating the deterministic lower bound of 22. On inputs without self-overlap, our bound improves on FER’s guarantee for 2≤k≤72\leq k\leq 7 and matches it at k=8k=8.

Theorem 4.1.

For every integer k≥2k\geq 2 and every input σ\sigma of overlap at most kk with no self-overlap, against an oblivious adversary, WBIT satisfies

𝔼⁡[WBIT​(σ)]≤(134−92​(k+1))​OPT​(σ).\mathbb{E}[\textnormal{{WBIT}}(\sigma)]\leq\left(\frac{13}{4}-\frac{9}{2(k+1)}\right)\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma)\ .

When k=2k=2, the no-self-overlap assumption can be omitted.

4.1 Proof of Theorem 4.1

Fix k≥2k\geq 2 and an input of overlap at most kk with no self-overlap. Fix an optimal schedule independently of the initial bits.

We first recall previously established results and lemmas. By Lemma 3.3, we may assume that OPT uses no free exchanges. We use the notation of Section 2.3 with ALG=WBIT\mathrm{ALG}=\textnormal{{WBIT}}, so since WBIT always serves a request at its deadline, tiWBIT=dit_{i}^{\textnormal{{WBIT}}}=d_{i}. We continue to use the convention in Section 3.2.2 to order the actions of OPT and WBIT when they happen at the same time step. Lemma 3.5 applies here as well: each element has at most one pre-served request, and WBIT does not access eie_{i} during σi\sigma_{i}’s pre-service interval before serving σi\sigma_{i}. Indeed, any other such request would have a window intersecting [ri,di][r_{i},d_{i}].

The event sequence and the pre-service intervals are independent of the initial bits. At any fixed event, the current bit of an element is its initial bit XOR the parity of a fixed number of preceding accesses. The current bits are therefore independent and uniform. They need not be independent of WBIT’s list order.

4.1.1 The potential function.

As in Section 3.2, the potential function deposits credit when OPT pre-serves a request and accumulates credits in the μ\mu and ν\nu accounts to pay for WBIT’s later service of the request.

Set

C=134−92​(k+1),δ=92​(k+1).C=\frac{13}{4}-\frac{9}{2(k+1)},\qquad\delta=\frac{9}{2(k+1)}.

We use the potential function

Φ=φ+∑i:σi​ pre-served(Cyi+∑f≠ei(μi,f+νi,f)).\Phi=\varphi+\sum_{i:\,\sigma_{i}\text{ pre-served}}\left(Cy_{i}+\sum_{f\neq e_{i}}(\mu_{i,f}+\nu_{i,f})\right).

Here φ\varphi is the weighted inversion term, C​yiCy_{i} is the deposit for σi\sigma_{i}, and μi,f,νi,f\mu_{i,f},\nu_{i,f} are its credits associated with element ff. We motivate and define these terms in more detail next.

Recall that an inversion is an unordered pair of distinct elements {e,f}\{e,f\} where e≺OPTfe\prec_{\textnormal{{OPT}}}f and f≺WBITef\prec_{\textnormal{{WBIT}}}e. We now give every inversion pair a weight defined with bit⁡(e)\operatorname{bit}(e). Each inversion (e,f)(e,f) has weight 1+be,1+b_{e}, where be=bit⁡(e)b_{e}=\operatorname{bit}(e), and we define

φ=∑e≺OPTff≺WBITe(1+be).\varphi=\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}e\prec_{\textnormal{{OPT}}}f\\ f\prec_{\textnormal{{WBIT}}}e\end{subarray}}(1+b_{e}).

The weights attached to the inversions allow a WBIT’s access to release potential even when bit⁡(e)=1\operatorname{bit}(e)=1. In this case where the element requested is not moved to the front and the inversion remains, bit⁡(e)\operatorname{bit}(e) flips from 1 to 0, still releasing one unit to pay for the access.

The deposit C​yiCy_{i} carries a multiple of OPT’s payment for σi\sigma_{i} forward to WBIT’s later service. As in Section 3.2.2, let FiF_{i} be the yi−1y_{i}-1 predecessors of eie_{i} when OPT serves σi\sigma_{i}. Elements outside FiF_{i} may move ahead of eie_{i} in OPT before WBIT serves it. The accounts μi,f\mu_{i,f} and νi,f\nu_{i,f} collect credits to pay for these new predecessors for each request–element pair (σi,f)(\sigma_{i},f), with f≠eif\neq e_{i}: μi,f\mu_{i,f} records credits from OPT’s backward swaps of eie_{i} across ff, and νi,f\nu_{i,f} records credits from WBIT’s forward moves of ff across eie_{i}. We keep the credits for each ff separate because its contribution to the later access calculation depends on its own bit value.

When OPT serves σi\sigma_{i}, create a deposit C​yiCy_{i} and initialize μi,f=νi,f=0\mu_{i,f}=\nu_{i,f}=0 for every f≠eif\neq e_{i}. During eie_{i}’s pre-service interval, update the accounts as follows:

  • •

    When OPT moves eie_{i} backward across ff in a paid adjacent swap, add to μi,f\mu_{i,f} the amount

    Δ​μi,f={C+1,f≺WBITei,C−1−bf,ei≺WBITf.\Delta\mu_{i,f}=\begin{cases}C+1,&f\prec_{\textnormal{{WBIT}}}e_{i},\\ C-1-b_{f},&e_{i}\prec_{\textnormal{{WBIT}}}f.\end{cases}
  • •

    When a WBIT access to ff moves ff forward across eie_{i}, add δ\delta to νi,f\nu_{i,f} if f≺OPTeif\prec_{\textnormal{{OPT}}}e_{i}.

When WBIT serves σi\sigma_{i}, remove its deposit C​yiCy_{i} and all credits μi,f,νi,f\mu_{i,f},\nu_{i,f} for f≠eif\neq e_{i} from the potential.

We show at every fixed event that

𝔼⁡[Δ​WBIT+Δ​Φ]≤C​Δ​OPT.\mathbb{E}[\Delta\textnormal{{WBIT}}+\Delta\Phi]\leq C\,\Delta\textnormal{{OPT}}.

Here each Δ\Delta denotes the change during the event under consideration, and bits and list orders are evaluated immediately before that event. All expectations are over the initial bits, without conditioning on WBIT’s current list or its preceding random choices.

When OPT serves σi\sigma_{i}, it pays yiy_{i} and changes no list order. Only the deposit C​yiCy_{i} is created. Thus Δ​WBIT+Δ​Φ=C​yi=C​Δ​OPT\Delta\textnormal{{WBIT}}+\Delta\Phi=Cy_{i}=C\Delta\textnormal{{OPT}}.

When OPT makes a paid adjacent swap, there are two cases depending on whether the backward-moving element has a pre-served request. Suppose first that OPT moves an element eie_{i} with pre-served request backward across ff. No self-overlap ensures that only one request to eie_{i} is pre-served, so only μi,f\mu_{i,f} receives an increment of Δ​μi,f\Delta\mu_{i,f}. Δ​Φ=Δ​φ+Δ​μi,f=(1+bf)+(C−1−bf)=C.\Delta\Phi=\Delta\varphi+\Delta\mu_{i,f}=(1+b_{f})+(C-1-b_{f})=C.

When WBIT serves σi\sigma_{i}, it incurs the access cost and updates the inversion term, while also removing the deposit C​yiCy_{i} and all credits μi,f,νi,f\mu_{i,f},\nu_{i,f} for f≠eif\neq e_{i}.

ΔWBIT+ΔΦ=ΔWBIT+Δφ−Cyi−∑f≠ei(μi,f+νi,f)+∑j≠iσj​ pre-servedΔνj,ei.\displaystyle\Delta\textnormal{{WBIT}}+\Delta\Phi=\Delta\textnormal{{WBIT}}+\Delta\varphi-Cy_{i}-\sum_{f\neq e_{i}}(\mu_{i,f}+\nu_{i,f})\quad+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\neq i\\ \sigma_{j}\text{ pre-served}\end{subarray}}\Delta\nu_{j,e_{i}}.

Here μi,f\mu_{i,f} and νi,f\nu_{i,f} are the balances immediately before the service. The last sum records the increase in νj,ei\nu_{j,e_{i}} when WBIT moves eie_{i} forward pass other elements eje_{j} that has pre-served requests.

By Lemma 4.3, for each f∈Nif\in N_{i}, removing σi\sigma_{i}’s accounts μi,f\mu_{i,f} and νi,f\nu_{i,f} at the time of WBIT’s service offsets the contribution Xei​(f)X_{e_{i}}(f) in expectation. These swaps are fixed independently of the bits, and each increment has expectation at least C−3/2≥0C-3/2\geq 0. Also, νi,f≥0\nu_{i,f}\geq 0. 4.1.3 Choice of the constant.

The case of at least two later accesses needs C+δ≥13/4C+\delta\geq 13/4, while issuing new crossing credits needs C≥1+δ⁡(k−1)/2C\geq 1+\delta(k-1)/2. Equating these gives

δ=92​(k+1),C=134−92​(k+1).\delta=\frac{9}{2(k+1)},\qquad C=\frac{13}{4}-\frac{9}{2(k+1)}.

4.2 Removing self-overlap when k=2k=2

For 22-overlap inputs, the intersection of two windows for the same element cannot meet any third request’s window. This allows us to remove self-overlap without changing WBIT’s access sequence or increasing the cost of OPT.

Lemma 4.4.

For every 22-overlap input σ\sigma, there is a 22-overlap input σ′\sigma^{\prime} with no self-overlap such that WBIT​(σ′)=WBIT​(σ).\textnormal{{WBIT}}(\sigma^{\prime})=\textnormal{{WBIT}}(\sigma). For every initial bit assignment, OPT​(σ′)≤OPT​(σ).\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma^{\prime})\leq\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma). The transformation is independent of the random bits and preserves the initial list.

Proof.

We first construct σ′\sigma^{\prime}. Consider any two overlapping requests σi\sigma_{i} and σj\sigma_{j} to the same element ee, with di<djd_{i}<d_{j} (assuming endpoints are disjoint, we handle tied endpoints at the end of the proof). Let a=min⁡{ri,rj},a=\min\{r_{i},r_{j}\}, b=max⁡{ri,rj}b=\max\{r_{i},r_{j}\}. Choose c>dic>d_{i} before the first release time or deadline of any request occurring after did_{i}. In particular, c<djc<d_{j}. Replace the windows of σi\sigma_{i} and σj\sigma_{j} respectively with [a,di][a,d_{i}] and [c,dj].[c,d_{j}]. Apply this replacement to the remaining overlapping pairs in deadline order, and call the resulting input σ′\sigma^{\prime}. Each step preserves 22-overlap and keeps previously processed requests free of self-overlap, so σ′\sigma^{\prime} has no self-overlap.

We next show that a single replacement preserves WBIT’s cost for every initial bit assignment and does not increase OPT’s cost. Applying these comparisons successively proves the lemma.

Since we preserve all requests’ deadlines and their requested elements, we preserve WBIT’s cost: WBIT​(σ)=WBIT​(σ′).\textnormal{{WBIT}}(\sigma)=\textnormal{{WBIT}}(\sigma^{\prime}).

Now to compare offline costs, take an optimal schedule for the original input and consider its two accesses serving σi\sigma_{i} and σj\sigma_{j}. Relabel the earlier access as the service of σi\sigma_{i}, and the later access as the service of σj\sigma_{j}. Since both requests are to the same element ee, this changes only the request labels, not the actions or their costs.

For the earlier access, it must lie in [a,di][a,d_{i}]: neither access can precede the earliest release time aa, and at least one must occur by did_{i} to serve the original σi.\sigma_{i}. Similarly, the later access must lie in [b,dj][b,d_{j}]: at least one access must be made at or after bb, and both requests must be served by djd_{j}. If the later access also lies in [c,dj],[c,d_{j}], then the schedule can also apply to our new input and we’re done. Otherwise, postpone this later access, any immediate free move, and all subsequent paid swaps before cc to time cc, preserving their order. By 22-overlap and the choice of cc, no third request’s window meets [b,c][b,c]. The postponement therefore delays no other request’s service, and σj\sigma_{j} is served feasibly at its new release cc. Since the order of all accesses and moves is unchanged, their costs are unchanged.

The constructed schedule is feasible for the modified input and has cost OPT​(σ)\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma). Hence the minimum feasible cost for that input satisfies OPT​(σ′)≤OPT​(σ)\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma^{\prime})\leq\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma).

To handle tied endpoints, choose ε>0\varepsilon>0 small enough that shifting endpoints by less than ε\varepsilon preserves the order of endpoints that originally occurred at different times. Move the releases at each time tt to distinct times in (t−ε,t)(t-\varepsilon,t), and the deadlines at tt to distinct times in (t,t+ε)(t,t+\varepsilon), ordered according to WBIT’s fixed, bit-independent tie order.

Keep every action of the original OPT schedule at its original time. Since releases move earlier and deadlines move later, every service remains within its request’s window. Thus the perturbation does not increase the optimal cost.

For WBIT, the new deadlines preserve the order of accesses. For any fixed initial bit assignment, the same access sequence produces the same bit flips and list movements. Each access therefore occurs at the same list position and incurs the same cost; only its time changes.

These changes do not increase overlap. Every window present within (t−ε,t+ε)(t-\varepsilon,t+\varepsilon) already contained tt in the original input. Outside these intervals, the windows are unchanged. All endpoints are now distinct, so we can apply the construction above.

∎

As a result, WBIT is 7/47/4-competitive on all 22-overlap inputs against an oblivious adversary, matching classical BIT’s guarantee [24] and below the deterministic lower bound of 22.

5 The Delay Model

Throughout this section, delay functions are nondecreasing, eventually divergent, and zero at release. Time in the delay model is continuous. An algorithm may access or swap elements at any nonnegative real time. These actions are instantaneous: they incur cost but take no time. In the delay-unaware setting, an algorithm continuously observes each pending request’s current delay but does not know its future delay. In the delay-aware setting, the entire delay function for a request is revealed when the request arrives.

5.1 A lower bound for delay-unaware algorithms

Theorem 5.1.

No deterministic delay-unaware algorithm for NBA list update with delays has a competitive ratio smaller than 2+32+\sqrt{3}.

Proof.

Fix a deterministic delay-unaware algorithm AA and a list with nn elements, with n≥2n\geq 2. We construct inputs with arbitrarily large mm requests, so that we rule out an additive constant depending on nn.

Construction.

We construct requests σ1,…,σm\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{m} recursively as AA runs. Request σi\sigma_{i} asks for element eie_{i}, is released at time rir_{i}, and has delay function fif_{i}. Let sis_{i} be the time at which AA serves it. Set r1=0r_{1}=0 and ri=si−1+1r_{i}=s_{i-1}+1 for 2≤i≤m2\leq i\leq m, and choose eie_{i} to be the last element in AA’s list immediately before σi\sigma_{i} is released. Thus AA has at most one pending request at a time. The times rir_{i} and sis_{i} need not be integers; the added unit only separates one request’s service from the next release.

The delay function of σi\sigma_{i} grows at unit rate until AA serves it, remains constant through time sm+1s_{m}+1, and then resumes unit-rate growth:

fi​(t)={t−ri,ri≤t<si,si−ri,si≤t≤sm+1,si−ri+t−(sm+1),t>sm+1.f_{i}(t)=\begin{cases}t-r_{i},&r_{i}\leq t<s_{i},\\ s_{i}-r_{i},&s_{i}\leq t\leq s_{m}+1,\\ s_{i}-r_{i}+t-(s_{m}+1),&t>s_{m}+1.\end{cases}

Each function is continuous, nondecreasing, zero at release, and eventually divergent.

Once the construction is complete, the displayed functions define a fixed input for both AA and OPT. Because AA is deterministic and delay-unaware, specifying the functions’ future values does not change the observations or decisions made during the construction.

We may assume that AA serves every released request. Otherwise, suppose it stops at request σi\sigma_{i}. Release no further requests and let its delay exceed C​n​i+bA​(n)Cni+b_{A}(n) for any claimed guarantee A⁡(σ)≤C​OPT​(σ)+bA​(n)A(\sigma)\leq C\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma)+b_{A}(n). At that point, let all earlier frozen functions resume unit-rate growth, so every delay function is eventually divergent. An offline schedule can serve the ii released requests immediately for total cost at most n​ini. Thus AA violates the guarantee if it eventually serves σi\sigma_{i}, and is infeasible if it never does. Hence every sis_{i} may be assumed finite.

Online cost.

By construction, every requested element is at position nn when its request arrives. Until that request is served by AA, it is the only request available for service. Neither paid swaps before the access or free forward movement after the access could reduce the access cost33 3 Paid swaps may lower the eventual access position, but each position gained costs one paid swap. Free forward movement occurs only after the access and therefore cannot reduce the cost when serving the current request.. Thus the access and preceding movement cost at least nn per request. These pending intervals are disjoint, so no swap is charged twice. If Δ\Delta denotes the total delay paid by AA, then

A⁡(σ)≥n​m+Δ.A(\sigma)\geq nm+\Delta. (5)
Offline cost.

We now construct an offline schedule for the input σ\sigma defined above by AA. It serves requests to some elements immediately and postpones requests to the others. Postponement lets it serve all requests to one element consecutively at position 11, while the constant segments of the delay functions prevent any additional delay cost after AA’s service.

Consider any ordering of the nn elements; we will use averaging later to show that some ordering gives the desired cost bound. At time 00, arrange the offline list in this order using at most (n2)\binom{n}{2} paid adjacent swaps. The first ℓ\ell elements in this order are the ones whose requests we serve immediately at release, 1≤ℓ<n1\leq\ell<n. We will choose ℓ\ell’s value after calculating the cost. The schedule then proceeds as follows.

  1. 1.

    Before time sm+1s_{m}+1, serve each request to one of the first ℓ\ell elements at its release time, without changing the list. Postpone all other requests until time sm+1s_{m}+1.

    For a particular ordering, its total cost is

    ∑j=1ℓj⋅(# of requests to the element at position j).\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}j\cdot\text{(\# of requests to the element at position $j$)}.
  2. 2.

    At time sm+1s_{m}+1, serve all requests postponed previously one at a time. Choose an element with pending requests, move it to the front using at most n−1n-1 paid adjacent swaps, and then serve every pending request to it by a separate access at position 11. Continue with the next element until all postponed requests have been served. All these actions occur at time sm+1s_{m}+1, in the stated order, without advancing time.

    Each element is moved at most once, so the total movement cost is at most (n−ℓ)​(n−1)(n-\ell)(n-1). Each postponed request σi\sigma_{i} pays one unit for access and delay fi​(sm+1)=si−rif_{i}(s_{m}+1)=s_{i}-r_{i}, equal to its delay under AA. Its access and delay costs therefore total 1+si−ri1+s_{i}-r_{i}.

The schedule above is feasible for every ordering, but its cost depends on which elements occupy the first ℓ\ell positions. To upper-bound OPT, we only need one ordering for which this cost is small. We show that such an ordering exists by averaging the total cost over all orderings with equal weight: at least one ordering costs no more than this average.

Before sm+1s_{m}+1, for each request, if its requested element has location j≤ℓj\leq\ell, it costs jj, otherwise it costs 0. For each requested element, it occupies position jj in fraction 1n\frac{1}{n} of all possible orderings. Summing over all mm requests, the average cost before time sm+1s_{m}+1 is

mn​∑j=1ℓj=ℓ⁡(ℓ+1)2​n​m.\frac{m}{n}\sum_{j=1}^{\ell}j=\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{2n}\,m.

In a fraction 1−ℓ/n1-\ell/n of the orderings, the service of request σi\sigma_{i} is postponed to sm+1s_{m}+1, where its access and delay cost is 1+si−ri1+s_{i}-r_{i}. Since ∑i=1m(si−ri)=Δ\sum_{i=1}^{m}(s_{i}-r_{i})=\Delta (recall Δ\Delta is the total delay paid by AA), the average access and delay cost at time sm+1s_{m}+1 is

(1−ℓn)​∑i=1m(1+si−ri)=(1−ℓn)​(m+Δ).\left(1-\frac{\ell}{n}\right)\sum_{i=1}^{m}(1+s_{i}-r_{i})=\left(1-\frac{\ell}{n}\right)(m+\Delta).

The paid swaps, both initially to form the ordering and at time sm+1s_{m}+1, cost at most

(n2)+(n−ℓ)​(n−1)≤2​n2.\binom{n}{2}+(n-\ell)(n-1)\leq 2n^{2}.

This movement bound holds for every ordering.

Adding the three costs bounds the average total cost. Hence

OPT(σ)≤ℓ⁡(ℓ+1)2​n​m⏟Step 1+(1−ℓn)​(m+Δ)⏟Step 2: accesses and delay+2​n2⏟paid swaps.\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma)\leq\underbrace{\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{2n}\,m}_{\text{Step 1}}+\underbrace{\left(1-\frac{\ell}{n}\right)(m+\Delta)}_{\text{Step 2: accesses and delay}}+\underbrace{2n^{2}}_{\text{paid swaps}}. (6)

Now choose ℓ=⌊(3−1)​n⌋\ell=\lfloor(\sqrt{3}-1)n\rfloor. Then Equation 6 gives

OPT​(σ)≤(2−3+1n)​(n​m+Δ)+2​n2.\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma)\leq\left(2-\sqrt{3}+\frac{1}{n}\right)(nm+\Delta)+2n^{2}. (7)

To verify (7), bound the coefficients of mm (access costs) and Δ\Delta (delay costs) in (6):

ℓ⁡(ℓ+1)2​n+1−ℓn\displaystyle\frac{\ell(\ell+1)}{2n}+1-\frac{\ell}{n} =1+ℓ⁡(ℓ−1)2​n≤(2−3)​n+1,\displaystyle=1+\frac{\ell(\ell-1)}{2n}\leq(2-\sqrt{3})n+1,
1−ℓn\displaystyle 1-\frac{\ell}{n} ≤2−3+1n.\displaystyle\leq 2-\sqrt{3}+\frac{1}{n}.

We next conclude that the competitive ratio has the lower bound of 2+3.2+\sqrt{3}. Suppose for contradiction that AA had competitive factor C<2+3C<2+\sqrt{3}. This would mean

A⁡(σ)≤C​OPT​(σ)+bA​(n)for every input ​σ,A(\sigma)\leq C\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma)+b_{A}(n)\qquad\text{for every input }\sigma,

where bA​(n)b_{A}(n) is finite and may depend on AA and nn, but not on the request sequence or its length mm. Since C⁡(2−3)<1C(2-\sqrt{3})<1, choose nn large enough that C⁡(2−3+1/n)<1C(2-\sqrt{3}+1/n)<1, and then keep this nn fixed. Combining the claimed guarantee with (5) and (7) would require

[1−C⁡(2−3+1n)]​(n​m+Δ)≤2​C​n2+bA​(n).\left[1-C\left(2-\sqrt{3}+\frac{1}{n}\right)\right](nm+\Delta)\leq 2Cn^{2}+b_{A}(n).

Fixing nn keeps the entire right-hand side fixed, including the additive constant. The bracket is positive and Δ≥0\Delta\geq 0, so increasing mm makes the left-hand side arbitrarily large, a contradiction. ∎

5.2 Delayed Move-to-Front

We again use move-to-front, but now the accumulated delay determines when to access an element. Let Re​(t)R_{e}(t) denote the set of pending requests to ee, and let ce​(t)=∑σi∈Re​(t)fi​(t)c_{e}(t)=\sum_{\sigma_{i}\in R_{e}(t)}f_{i}(t) be the total delay across all requests in the set. DMF, presented in Algorithm 3, is delay-unaware and serves one request to ee as soon as ce​(t)c_{e}(t) reaches 2/32/3 of its current position. It moves ee to the front for free and serves all remaining requests on it with a cost of 1 each.

The accumulated delay cost ce​(t)c_{e}(t) may reach the triggering condition simultaneously for different elements. We use any fixed tie-breaking, and each time after the move-to-front, the element positions are recomputed and the triggering condition might change accordingly.

In the delay-aware extension, we also allow left-continuous delay functions with jumps. Since the functions are known at release, DMF serves at the threshold-crossing time; if a jump would carry the delay above the threshold, it serves at the jump time, before the higher value applies.

The proof of Lemma 3.3 also applies to the delay model: the transformation preserves every service time, so all delay costs remain unchanged. Thus, we may assume that OPT uses no free exchanges.

Theorem 5.2.

For continuous, nondecreasing, divergent delay functions with fi​(ri)=0f_{i}(r_{i})=0, the 2/32/3-threshold algorithm DMF is 55-competitive in the delay-unaware model. Its delay-aware extension is also 55-competitive for left-continuous functions.

Proof.

We compare DMF and OPT on the same input. The two schedules may serve requests at different times and maintain different list orders. We use a potential to account for these differences and prove that DMF’s total cost is at most five times OPT’s. We first prove the bound for continuous delay functions in the delay-unaware regime. We then extend the proof to left-continuous delay functions with jumps in the delay-aware regime, where each function is known in full at release.

Before defining the potential, we calculate DMF’s cost for each group of requests it serves together. We then construct a comparison schedule OPT∗\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*} with one offline access per group and identify the inequality that the potential must establish.

We designed DMF such that it waits until the total delay of the pending requests to some element ee reaches two-thirds of ee’s current position. It then serves all pending requests to ee at that time. We call the set of these actions on ee one service event. Index the events by j=1,…,Jj=1,\ldots,J. At event jj, let eje_{j} be the element served, RjR_{j} its set of pending requests, tjt_{j} the service time, and xjx_{j} its position just before service. DMF serves one request by accessing eje_{j} at cost xjx_{j}, moves eje_{j} to the front for free, and serves each of the other |Rj|−1|R_{j}|-1 requests by a separate access at cost 11. We observe that

∑σi∈Rjfi​(tj)=23​xj,∑σi∈Rjfi​(u)≥23​xjfor every ​u>tj.\sum_{\sigma_{i}\in R_{j}}f_{i}(t_{j})=\frac{2}{3}x_{j},\qquad\sum_{\sigma_{i}\in R_{j}}f_{i}(u)\geq\frac{2}{3}x_{j}\quad\text{for every }u>t_{j}. (8)

The first equality follows from the definition of the service time, and the second inequality follows from monotonicity.

Thus DMF’s cost at event jj is at most 53​xj+(|Rj|−1)\frac{5}{3}x_{j}+(|R_{j}|-1). Let M=∑j(|Rj|−1)M=\sum_{j}(|R_{j}|-1) count all the accesses made after moving an element to the front. Summing the event costs gives

DMF​(σ)≤∑j53​xj+M.\textnormal{{DMF}}(\sigma)\leq\sum_{j}\frac{5}{3}x_{j}+M. (9)

We now construct OPT∗\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*}. By Lemma 3.3, we may assume that OPT uses no free exchanges. We can therefore delete an offline access without changing the list or the positions of later accesses. For each set of requests RjR_{j}, keep only the first access by OPT that serves a request σ^j\hat{\sigma}_{j} in RjR_{j} and delete all other services to requests in RjR_{j}. Let τj\tau_{j} be the time at which OPT serves σ^j\hat{\sigma}_{j}, and let yjy_{j} be the position of eje_{j} in OPT at time τj\tau_{j}. Keep every paid swap, and preserve the times and order of all retained actions. Call this reduced schedule OPT∗\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*}.

In OPT∗\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*}, assign the retained access the delay charge

{0,τj≤tj,23​xj,τj>tj.\begin{cases}0,&\tau_{j}\leq t_{j},\\ \frac{2}{3}x_{j},&\tau_{j}>t_{j}.\end{cases}

OPT∗\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*}’s delay defined above never exceeds OPT’s total delay for RjR_{j}. The zero case is immediate. In the other case, every request in RjR_{j} is served by OPT at or after τj>tj\tau_{j}>t_{j}, so their total delay is at least ∑σi∈Rjfi​(τj)≥23​xj\sum_{\sigma_{i}\in R_{j}}f_{i}(\tau_{j})\geq\frac{2}{3}x_{j} by (8).

Consider the cost of OPT∗\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*}, also denoted OPT∗\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*}. Note that we use this quantity only for comparison; we do not run DMF on a modified input. Exactly MM offline accesses were deleted, each costing at least 11, and neither the remaining access costs nor the delay charges increased. Consequently,

OPT∗≤OPT​(σ)−M.\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*}\leq\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma)-M. (10)

Hence, to show that DMF(σ)(\sigma) is 5-competitive, it suffices to prove

∑j53​xj≤5​OPT∗;\sum_{j}\frac{5}{3}x_{j}\leq 5\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*}; (11)

since together with the two cost bounds above, this inequality gives DMF​(σ)≤5​OPT∗+M≤5​(OPT​(σ)−M)+M≤5​OPT​(σ)\textnormal{{DMF}}(\sigma)\leq 5\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*}+M\leq 5(\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma)-M)+M\leq 5\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma).

The potential.

We examine the actions of DMF and OPT∗\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*} in chronological order. When both schedules act at the same time, put all OPT∗\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*} actions before all DMF actions, preserving each schedule’s internal order. Thus the retained offline access for group RjR_{j} comes before DMF exactly when τj≤tj\tau_{j}\leq t_{j}.

We define our potential as follows:

Φ=53​φ+∑j∈𝒫(5​yj+μj)−∑j∈ℒ103​xj.\Phi=\frac{5}{3}\varphi+\sum_{j\in\mathcal{P}}(5y_{j}+\mu_{j})-\sum_{j\in\mathcal{L}}\frac{10}{3}x_{j}. (12)

We define its terms below.

Inversions φ\varphi: An inversion is an unordered pair of elements appearing in opposite orders in the DMF and OPT∗\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*} lists (OPT∗\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*} list is the same as OPT list). Let φ\varphi count these pairs.

It starts at zero at the retained offline access. While the group is pre-served, increase μj\mu_{j} by 103\frac{10}{3} whenever a paid swap by OPT∗\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*} moves eje_{j} one position backward.

Note that the set RjR_{j} contributes in total 5​yj+μj5y_{j}+\mu_{j}. When DMF serves RjR_{j}, we remove both the deposit and the account, so their decrease can offset DMF’s cost.

Unlike the preceding upper-bound proofs, in which the online algorithm always acts at deadlines, here we face the possibility that DMF may serve the group before OPT∗.\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*}. Let ℒ\mathcal{L} contain the indices jj for which DMF has served RjR_{j} but the retained offline access has not yet occurred. For each j∈ℒj\in\mathcal{L}, include the negative term −103​xj-\frac{10}{3}x_{j}, where xjx_{j} is the position of eje_{j} in DMF at DMF’s service. Adding this term decreases the potential when DMF serves the group. Keep it until the retained offline access and remove it at OPT∗\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*}’s access, increasing the potential by 103​xj\frac{10}{3}x_{j}.

Observe that the potential may be negative during the execution. We only need its endpoint values: initially it is zero because the lists agree and neither schedule has served any requests; after both finish, 𝒫\mathcal{P} and ℒ\mathcal{L} are empty, so Φfinal=53​φ≥0\Phi_{\mathrm{final}}=\frac{5}{3}\varphi\geq 0.

Comparing costs at each action.

Let Δ​D\Delta\mathrm{D} be 53​xj\frac{5}{3}x_{j} at DMF’s event jj and zero at other actions (since we’re excluding MM here). Let Δ​OPT∗\Delta\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*} be the cost charged to the reduced schedule at the action. We will prove

Δ​D+Δ​Φ≤5​Δ​OPT∗.\Delta\mathrm{D}+\Delta\Phi\leq 5\,\Delta\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*}. (13)

Summing this inequality will cancel all intermediate potential values and give (11). There are three action types. Observe that, although delay accumulates continuously, it is charged only at service and does not appear in the potential. Releases also change neither the charged cost nor the potential. It therefore suffices to consider the following three action types.

1. A retained offline access to request in RjR_{j}.

If DMF has not yet served RjR_{j}, then jj enters 𝒫\mathcal{P}. We add 5​yj5y_{j} to the potential and start μj\mu_{j} at zero. Neither list changes, and the assigned delay is zero, so

Δ​D+Δ​Φ=5​yj=5​Δ​OPT∗.\Delta\mathrm{D}+\Delta\Phi=5y_{j}=5\,\Delta\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*}.

If DMF has already served RjR_{j}, then jj leaves ℒ\mathcal{L}. Removing its negative term increases the potential by 103​xj\frac{10}{3}x_{j}. Here τj>tj\tau_{j}>t_{j}, and therefore

Δ​D+Δ​Φ=103​xj≤5​(yj+23​xj)=5​Δ​OPT∗.\Delta\mathrm{D}+\Delta\Phi=\frac{10}{3}x_{j}\leq 5\left(y_{j}+\frac{2}{3}x_{j}\right)=5\,\Delta\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*}.
2. A paid offline swap.

An adjacent swap changes only the swapped pair’s inversion status, so the inversion term increases by at most 53\frac{5}{3}. We must also bound the increase in the μ\mu accounts.

Only accounts for the backward-moving element can increase. There is at most one: DMF clears all pending requests to that element, so requests in its next group arrive strictly after that service. The old account is therefore removed before the next group’s retained offline access can create a new one.

If the backward-moving element has a pre-served group, its account increases by 103\frac{10}{3}; otherwise no account changes. All other terms are fixed. Since the swap costs one,

Δ​D+Δ​Φ≤53+103=5=5​Δ​OPT∗.\Delta\mathrm{D}+\Delta\Phi\leq\frac{5}{3}+\frac{10}{3}=5=5\,\Delta\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*}.
3. A DMF service event.

At event jj, DMF serves RjR_{j} and moves eje_{j} from position xjx_{j} to the front. The charge Δ​D\Delta\mathrm{D} is 53​xj\frac{5}{3}x_{j}, and OPT∗\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*} pays nothing at this action. We must therefore show that Δ​D+Δ​Φ≤0\Delta\mathrm{D}+\Delta\Phi\leq 0. Only the inversion term and the term for group RjR_{j} can change. We distinguish whether the retained offline access for this group has already occurred.

Case 1: the retained offline access has not yet occurred. There is no deposit or account to remove. Instead, jj enters ℒ\mathcal{L}, adding −103​xj-\frac{10}{3}x_{j} to the potential. The move to the front creates at most xj−1x_{j}-1 inversions, so

Δ​D+Δ​Φ≤53​xj+53​(xj−1)−103​xj=−53≤0.\Delta\mathrm{D}+\Delta\Phi\leq\frac{5}{3}x_{j}+\frac{5}{3}(x_{j}-1)-\frac{10}{3}x_{j}=-\frac{5}{3}\leq 0.

Case 2: the retained offline access has already occurred. Here j∈𝒫j\in\mathcal{P}. DMF’s service removes the term 5​yj+μj5y_{j}+\mu_{j} from the potential, where μj\mu_{j} is its balance immediately before service. We will use this decrease to cover the service charge of DMF and the change in inversions.

Let AjA_{j} be the elements ahead of eje_{j} in both lists immediately before this event. Moving eje_{j} to the front creates an inversion with each element in AjA_{j}. Each of its other xj−1−|Aj|x_{j}-1-|A_{j}| online predecessors is behind eje_{j} offline, so moving past it removes an inversion. Including the removal of the group’s deposit and account, the full change is

Δ​D+Δ​Φ\displaystyle\Delta\mathrm{D}+\Delta\Phi =53​xj+53​Δ​φ−5​yj−μj\displaystyle=\frac{5}{3}x_{j}+\frac{5}{3}\Delta\varphi-5y_{j}-\mu_{j}
=53​xj+53​(|Aj|−(xj−1−|Aj|))−5​yj−μj\displaystyle=\frac{5}{3}x_{j}+\frac{5}{3}\bigl(|A_{j}|-(x_{j}-1-|A_{j}|)\bigr)-5y_{j}-\mu_{j}
=103​|Aj|+53−5​yj−μj.\displaystyle=\frac{10}{3}|A_{j}|+\frac{5}{3}-5y_{j}-\mu_{j}. (14)

Thus we only need to account for the elements in AjA_{j}.

To do this, let FjF_{j} be the set of elements ahead of eje_{j} at its retained offline access. This set records the list at that earlier access and stays fixed; |Fj|=yj−1|F_{j}|=y_{j}-1. Split AjA_{j} into two parts:

  • •

    Elements already ahead at the offline access. These are the elements of Aj∩FjA_{j}\cap F_{j}, of which there are at most yj−1y_{j}-1. They are the elements covered by the deposit 5​yj5y_{j}.

  • •

    Elements that became offline predecessors later. Each f∈Aj∖Fjf\in A_{j}\setminus F_{j} was behind eje_{j} at the retained offline access and is ahead of it now. Since OPT∗\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*} changes its list only through paid adjacent swaps, an intervening swap must have moved eje_{j} backward past ff. The group was pre-served at that swap, so μj\mu_{j} increased by 103\frac{10}{3}. Different elements require different swaps, and the account never decreases. Therefore

    μj≥103​|Aj∖Fj|.\mu_{j}\geq\frac{10}{3}|A_{j}\setminus F_{j}|.

    This includes swaps after the retained access at the same time as DMF’s service: all offline actions at that time precede DMF’s event in the analysis.

Subtracting μj\mu_{j} therefore covers all the new predecessors in the second part, leaving only those already present at the offline access:

103​|Aj|−μj≤103​|Aj∩Fj|≤103​(yj−1).\frac{10}{3}|A_{j}|-\mu_{j}\leq\frac{10}{3}|A_{j}\cap F_{j}|\leq\frac{10}{3}(y_{j}-1).

Substituting into (14), the deposit covers these remaining terms:

Δ​D+Δ​Φ≤103​(yj−1)+53−5​yj=−53​(yj+1)≤0.\Delta\mathrm{D}+\Delta\Phi\leq\frac{10}{3}(y_{j}-1)+\frac{5}{3}-5y_{j}=-\frac{5}{3}(y_{j}+1)\leq 0.
Concluding the cost bound.

Summing (13) over all actions gives

∑j53​xj+Φfinal−Φinitial≤5​OPT∗.\sum_{j}\frac{5}{3}x_{j}+\Phi_{\mathrm{final}}-\Phi_{\mathrm{initial}}\leq 5\textnormal{{OPT}}^{*}.

Since Φinitial=0\Phi_{\mathrm{initial}}=0 and Φfinal≥0\Phi_{\mathrm{final}}\geq 0, this proves (11).

Delay-aware extension with non-continuous delay functions.

A jump in our delay function might skip our 23​xi\frac{2}{3}x_{i} threshold. We consider a delay-aware version of DMF that knows the functions at release, and hence allows service at the time of the jump. On the other hand, left-continuity ensures that the lower delay value still applies. We choose service times that preserve the two delay bounds in (8) when the functions are left-continuous and known in full at release.

The service actions of the delay-aware DMF remain the same; only the rule for choosing their times changes. At a time tt, let Re​(t)R_{e}(t) be the pending requests to ee, whose current position is xx. For each nonempty Re​(t)R_{e}(t), compute

de=inf{u≥t:∑σi∈Re​(t)fi​(u)≥23​x}.d_{e}=\inf\left\{u\geq t:\sum_{\sigma_{i}\in R_{e}(t)}f_{i}(u)\geq\frac{2}{3}x\right\}.

The infimum need not belong to the set: at a jump, the delay may still be below the threshold at ded_{e} and exceed it immediately afterward. Service at the real time ded_{e} is allowed and pays the value at ded_{e}.

DMF plans to serve an element with the smallest ded_{e}, breaking ties by the fixed order. If new requests arrive at or before that time, it processes all releases at that time and recomputes every ded_{e} using the updated pending sets. It also recomputes after each service, using the updated list positions. All computations use only the delay functions of currently pending requests.

Delay at DMF’s service. We show that, for each element, the total delay of its pending requests never exceeds its current threshold. Pending delay starts at zero. Arrivals add zero delay, and a service clears the served element’s pending set without lowering other thresholds. DMF never waits past the smallest ded_{e}, where left-continuity keeps the delay at most the threshold. Hence

∑σi∈Rjfi​(tj)≤23​xj.\sum_{\sigma_{i}\in R_{j}}f_{i}(t_{j})\leq\frac{2}{3}x_{j}.

Delay at a later time. Since each delay function is nondecreasing, the total delay of the fixed group RjR_{j} is also nondecreasing. Fix the same group RjR_{j} and a time u>tju>t_{j}. If its total delay were still below 23​xj\frac{2}{3}x_{j} at uu, monotonicity would keep it below this threshold from the last recomputation through uu. The infimum defining its service time would then be at least uu, contradicting service at tj<ut_{j}<u. Therefore

∑σi∈Rjfi​(u)≥23​xj(u>tj).\sum_{\sigma_{i}\in R_{j}}f_{i}(u)\geq\frac{2}{3}x_{j}\qquad(u>t_{j}).

These are (8), so the preceding cost and potential analysis still gives factor 55. With continuous functions, the rule reduces to the original equality trigger. Every request is eventually served. Otherwise, an unserved request’s delay would eventually exceed 2​n/32n/3, contradicting the bound on the total pending delay at its element. ∎

Why the threshold is 2/32/3.

Suppose the threshold were θ​x\theta x, with θ>0\theta>0. With continuous delays, the first access and delay would cost (1+θ)​x(1+\theta)x. Keeping the same potential form replaces 53\frac{5}{3} by 1+θ1+\theta and 103\frac{10}{3} by 2​(1+θ)2(1+\theta). For a proposed competitive factor CC, use deposits C​yjCy_{j}. Two offline events determine the bound:

  • •

    A paid swap costs one and increases the inversion term and one account by at most (1+θ)+2​(1+θ)(1+\theta)+2(1+\theta). Thus it suffices to have C≥3​(1+θ)C\geq 3(1+\theta).

  • •

    If DMF serves first, the later offline access removes a negative term, increasing the potential by 2​(1+θ)​x2(1+\theta)x. Its assigned delay θ​x\theta x covers this increase after multiplication by CC if C​θ​x≥2​(1+θ)​xC\theta x\geq 2(1+\theta)x.

Thus the proof gives the bound

C=max⁡{3​(1+θ),2​(1+θ)θ}.C=\max\left\{3(1+\theta),\frac{2(1+\theta)}{\theta}\right\}.

The first expression increases with θ\theta, while the second, 2+2/θ2+2/\theta, decreases. Their maximum is smallest where they are equal:

3(1+θ)=2​(1+θ)θ⟺3θ=2.3(1+\theta)=\frac{2(1+\theta)}{\theta}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad 3\theta=2.

Hence θ=2/3\theta=2/3, and both expressions equal 55. This minimizes the bound supplied by this potential analysis.

Nonzero delay at release.

If fi​(ri)>0f_{i}(r_{i})>0 is allowed, run the algorithm on the residual functions f¯i​(t)=fi​(t)−fi​(ri)\bar{f}_{i}(t)=f_{i}(t)-f_{i}(r_{i}). Every schedule pays the unavoidable amount B=∑ifi​(ri)B=\sum_{i}f_{i}(r_{i}). Adding this amount back to the residual bound gives

DMFf≤B+5​OPTf¯≤5​OPTf.\textnormal{{DMF}}_{f}\leq B+5\textnormal{{OPT}}_{\bar{f}}\leq 5\textnormal{{OPT}}_{f}.

Thus the factor is unchanged when the trigger uses delay accumulated since release.
