Appendix A Omitted Material from Section 3

A.1 Counterexamples for simple serving orders

See 3.1

Proof of part (a).

First, we construct the counterexample for any deterministic ALG that always serves requests at their deadlines. Let the initial list be (e1,…,en)(e_{1},\dots,e_{n}).

All n2n^{2} requests arrive at time 00, and request σi\sigma_{i} has deadline di=id_{i}=i. Partition the requests into groups G1,⋯,GnG_{1},\cdots,G_{n} where Gg={σ1+(g−1)​n,σ2+(g−1)​n,⋯,σg​n}.G_{g}=\{\sigma_{1+(g-1)n},\sigma_{2+(g-1)n},\cdots,\sigma_{gn}\}. Each group contains one request to every element. In deadline order, the requested elements in GgG_{g} are

{(e1,e2,…,en),if ​g​ is odd,(en,en−1,…,e1),if ​g​ is even.\begin{cases}(e_{1},e_{2},\ldots,e_{n}),&\text{if }g\text{ is odd},\\ (e_{n},e_{n-1},\ldots,e_{1}),&\text{if }g\text{ is even}.\end{cases}

Thus, since ALG serves requests only at their deadlines, it must serve the groups consecutively, alternating between the forward and reverse order of the initial list.

We claim that each group costs ALG at least n⁡(n+1)/2n(n+1)/2. Each element starting at position jj in when we start serving the group would cost at least jj to serve and access (free moves of other elements won’t bring it forward, and paid exchanges bringing it forward can be charged to this element). The total cost of each group is therefore at least 1+2+⋯+n=Ω⁡(n2),1+2+\cdots+n=\Omega(n^{2}), and summing over nn groups,

ALG​(σ)≥n2​(n+1)2.\textsc{ALG}(\sigma)\geq\frac{n^{2}(n+1)}{2}.

OPT can instead serve all requests at time 00, grouping them by element. It first serves all requests to e1e_{1}, then all requests to e2e_{2}, and so on, moving each element to the front after its first access. Each element has nn requests. The first access to eje_{j} costs jj. Its remaining n−1n-1 accesses cost one each. Hence,

OPT​(σ)≤∑j=1n(j+n−1)=3​n2−n2,ALG​(σ)OPT​(σ)≥n⁡(n+1)3​n−1=Ω⁡(n).\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma)\leq\sum_{j=1}^{n}(j+n-1)=\frac{3n^{2}-n}{2},\qquad\frac{\textsc{ALG}(\sigma)}{\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma)}\geq\frac{n(n+1)}{3n-1}=\Omega(n).

Similarly, for an algorithm ALG that serves every request upon arrival, release the requests at times 1,…,n21,\ldots,n^{2} in the same order and give them all deadline n2+1n^{2}+1. The online algorithm again accesses every element once per group, so the same lower bound applies. Offline waits until time n2+1n^{2}+1 and serves the requests element by element using the schedule above, with the same cost. Thus the arrival-only rule also has competitive ratio Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n).

∎

Proof of part (b).

There are n2n^{2} requests in total, and we construct nn groups G1,…,GnG_{1},\ldots,G_{n}, each containing one request to every element. All requests in group GgG_{g} arrive at time 2​g−22g-2. Let e¯g\bar{e}_{g} be the last element in ALG’s list at this time. The request to e¯g\bar{e}_{g} has deadline 2​g−12g-1; the other requests have deadline 2​n2n.

At time 2​g−12g-1, ALG serves the entire group: first the requests to the preceding elements of e¯g\bar{e}_{g}, then the request to e¯g\bar{e}_{g}. Each group therefore requires one access to every element. By the counting argument in the previous proof, it costs ALG 1+2+⋯+n1+2+\dots+n per group, and hence in total,

ALG​(σ)≥n2​(n+1)2.\textsc{ALG}(\sigma)\geq\frac{n^{2}(n+1)}{2}.

OPT serves only the urgent request of each group at its deadline, without changing its list. These nn accesses cost at most n⋅n=n2n\cdot n=n^{2}. At time 2​n2n, it serves the remaining requests element by element, in initial list order, moving each element to the front after its first access. The remaining n2−nn^{2}-n requests cost at most n2−n+n⁡(n−1)/2n^{2}-n+n(n-1)/2. Thus

OPT​(σ)≤5​n2−3​n2,ALG​(σ)OPT​(σ)≥n⁡(n+1)5​n−3=Ω⁡(n).\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma)\leq\frac{5n^{2}-3n}{2},\qquad\frac{\textsc{ALG}(\sigma)}{\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma)}\geq\frac{n(n+1)}{5n-3}=\Omega(n).

∎

All lower bounds above also hold when an additive term β⁡(n)\beta(n) is allowed in the competitive ratio. Fix nn and repeat the construction on disjoint time intervals. Each repetition costs the online algorithm Ω⁡(n3)\Omega(n^{3}) and offline O⁡(n2)O(n^{2}), including the cost of restoring its list. Repeating sufficiently many times makes the fixed additive term β⁡(n)\beta(n) negligible, so the competitive-ratio lower bound remains Ω⁡(n)\Omega(n).

A.2 The lower bound for the family of algorithms including FER

This subsection proves Theorem 3.10 and Corollary A.4.

Recall that an algorithm is hh-local-lazy MTF if it uses no paid exchanges, moves every accessed element to the front, and serves requests early only within the first hh positions. We construct an input on which no request is ever eligible for early service.

Construction.

Fix 1≤h<n/21\leq h<n/2 and 1≤q≤n−h1\leq q\leq n-h. Relabel the initial list as L0=(en,…,e1)L_{0}=(e_{n},\ldots,e_{1}), so that e1e_{1} is initially last. We distinguish its first hh elements, its last qq elements, and the elements between them.

L0=(en,…,en−h+1⏟first ​h​ elements,en−h,…,eq+1⏟middle,eq,…,e1⏟last ​q​ elements).L_{0}=\bigl(\underbrace{e_{n},\ldots,e_{n-h+1}}_{\text{first }h\text{ elements}},\underbrace{e_{n-h},\ldots,e_{q+1}}_{\text{middle}},\underbrace{e_{q},\ldots,e_{1}}_{\text{last }q\text{ elements}}\bigr).

The instance In,q(h)I^{(h)}_{n,q} has a main request MℓM_{\ell} to each element eℓe_{\ell} (1≤ℓ≤n1\leq\ell\leq n), and an extra request EℓE_{\ell} to each of the last qq elements eℓe_{\ell} (1≤ℓ≤q1\leq\ell\leq q) of L0L_{0}. We choose release times to prevent early service: along a deadline execution, each request arrives only when its element is outside the first hh positions. Formally, the requests are

Mℓ=(eℓ,rℓ,2​ℓ)(1≤ℓ≤n),rℓ={0,ℓ≤n−h,2​(ℓ−(n−h))+1,ℓ>n−h,M_{\ell}=(e_{\ell},r_{\ell},2\ell)\quad(1\leq\ell\leq n),\qquad r_{\ell}=\begin{cases}0,&\ell\leq n-h,\\ 2\bigl(\ell-(n-h)\bigr)+1,&\ell>n-h,\end{cases}

and

Eℓ=(eℓ, 2​(ℓ+h)+1, 2​n+2​ℓ)(1≤ℓ≤q).E_{\ell}=(e_{\ell},\,2(\ell+h)+1,\,2n+2\ell)\qquad(1\leq\ell\leq q).

All windows are valid, since the main requests released at 0 have positive deadlines, and the other delayed main requests and the extra requests have window length 2​(n−h)−1>02(n-h)-1>0. For each 1≤ℓ≤q1\leq\ell\leq q, the extra request EℓE_{\ell} arrives after the main request MℓM_{\ell}’s deadline: 2​(ℓ+h)+1>2​ℓ2(\ell+h)+1>2\ell. Thus there is no self-overlap. Releases occur at zero or odd times and deadlines at distinct even times, so no tie-breaking convention is needed.

Online cost of AA. The next lemma shows that the release times force AA to follow the deadline order, accessing the last element each time.

Lemma A.1.

Every hh-local-lazy MTF algorithm AA serves all requests of In,q(h)I^{(h)}_{n,q} at their deadlines and at position nn. Hence

A⁡(In,q(h))=n⁡(n+q).A(I^{(h)}_{n,q})=n(n+q).
Proof.

Consider the execution that serves every request at its deadline and moves its element to the front. We will show that, throughout this execution, every alive request is to an element outside the first hh positions. Thus AA cannot make a first early access and must follow the same execution.

We first show that all requests served at deadlines have access cost nn. Note that for ℓ∈[n]\ell\in[n], at time 2​ℓ2\ell, before serving MℓM_{\ell}, the list is

(eℓ−1,…,e1,en,…,eℓ),(e_{\ell-1},\ldots,e_{1},\ e_{n},\ldots,e_{\ell}), (15)

so the requested element eℓe_{\ell} is always last. After M1,⋯,MnM_{1},\cdots,M_{n} are served, the list is restored to L0L_{0} at time 2​n2n. For ℓ∈[q],\ell\in[q], we then serve the extra requests EℓE_{\ell} at time 2​n+2​ℓ2n+2\ell, repeating the first qq accesses with the same pattern where eℓe_{\ell} is at the end when we serve EℓE_{\ell}.

In this execution, we first note that the element requested by each request is at position at least h+1h+1 when that request is released:

  • •

    For ℓ≤n−h\ell\leq n-h, MℓM_{\ell} is released when eℓe_{\ell} is at position n−ℓ+1≥h+1n-\ell+1\geq h+1.

  • •

    For ℓ>n−h\ell>n-h, let s=ℓ−(n−h)s=\ell-(n-h). Just before MℓM_{\ell}’s release at 2​s+12s+1, the first ss main accesses have pushed eℓe_{\ell} from position n−ℓ+1n-\ell+1 to position n−ℓ+1+s=h+1n-\ell+1+s=h+1.

  • •

    For ℓ∈[q]\ell\in[q], after eℓe_{\ell} is served at time 2​ℓ2\ell and moved to front, the next hh main accesses push it to position h+1h+1 before EℓE_{\ell} is released at time 2​(ℓ+h)+12(\ell+h)+1. These accesses exist because ℓ+h≤n\ell+h\leq n.

Since there is no self-overlap, no other request to the same element is served between a request’s release and its deadline. Moving other elements to the front cannot decrease its position. Thus every requested element remains outside the first hh positions from its release until its deadline access.

Because AA uses no paid exchanges and moves every accessed element to the front, its first deviation from this execution would have to be an early access. Immediately before that access, the two lists would agree, so the requested element would lie outside the permitted first hh positions, a contradiction. Hence AA follows this execution and pays nn for each of the n+qn+q requests. ∎

Cheaper offline schedule. To compare this cost with OPT, we now construct a feasible offline schedule. The schedule moves e1,⋯,eqe_{1},\cdots,e_{q} forward and serves their main requests in an order that prepares for cheaper extra accesses.

Lemma A.2.

On In,q(h)I^{(h)}_{n,q},

OPT​(In,q(h))≤n2+n+q2+q2+h​q.\textnormal{{OPT}}(I^{(h)}_{n,q})\leq\frac{n^{2}+n+q^{2}+q}{2}+hq.
Proof.

Consider the offline schedule that uses the following three stages.

  1. 1.

    At time 00, serve the middle requests and move e1,⋯,eqe_{1},\cdots,e_{q} forward. Serve Mn−h,…,Mq+1M_{n-h},\ldots,M_{q+1} without moving their elements. Their access positions are h+1,…,n−qh+1,\ldots,n-q. Next use q⁡(n−q−h)q(n-q-h) paid swaps to move the block (eq,⋯,e1)(e_{q},\cdots,e_{1}) immediately behind (en,⋯,en−h+1)(e_{n},\cdots,e_{n-h+1}), preserving the former’s internal order. The list becomes

    (en,…,en−h+1,eq,…,e1,en−h,…,eq+1).(e_{n},\ldots,e_{n-h+1},\ e_{q},\ldots,e_{1},\ e_{n-h},\ldots,e_{q+1}). (16)

    Serve M1M_{1} at position h+qh+q without moving it. We handle M1M_{1} separately because its deadline 22 precedes the next stage. Total cost in this stage is ∑p=h+1n−qp+q⁡(n−q−h)+h+q.\sum_{p=h+1}^{n-q}p+q(n-q-h)+h+q.

  2. 2.

    At time 33, arrange e1,⋯,eqe_{1},\cdots,e_{q} for their extra requests. Serve requests Mq,Mq−1,…,M2M_{q},M_{q-1},\ldots,M_{2}, moving each accessed element to the front. These requests were released at zero and have deadlines at least 44, so all these services are feasible. Their access positions are h+1,…,h+q−1h+1,\ldots,h+q-1. The list becomes

    (e2,…,eq,en,…,en−h+1,e1,en−h,…,eq+1).(e_{2},\ldots,e_{q},\ e_{n},\ldots,e_{n-h+1},\ e_{1},\ e_{n-h},\ldots,e_{q+1}). (17)

    Perform these accesses before serving Mn−h+1M_{n-h+1}, which is also released at time 33. Total cost in this stage is h⁡(q−1)+q⁡(q−1)2h(q-1)+\frac{q(q-1)}{2}.

  3. 3.

    Serve every remaining request at release, without moving. These are Mn−h+1,…,MnM_{n-h+1},\ldots,M_{n} and all extra requests. These main requests arrive at times 3,5,⋯,2​h+13,5,\cdots,2h+1, and every extra request arrives later, at time at least 2​h+32h+3. In (17), Mn−h+uM_{n-h+u} has access position q+h−uq+h-u for 1≤u≤h1\leq u\leq h. The position for E1E_{1} is h+qh+q, and that for EℓE_{\ell}, 2≤ℓ≤q2\leq\ell\leq q, is ℓ−1\ell-1. The list stays unchanged, so these positions hold at every remaining service. At this stage, serving these hh main requests costs h​q+h⁡(h−1)2hq+\frac{h(h-1)}{2}; and serving all extra requests cost h+q⁡(q+1)2h+\frac{q(q+1)}{2}.

The sum of costs over all stages is (n2+n+q2+q)/2+h​q(n^{2}+n+q^{2}+q)/2+hq, proving the bound. ∎

Lower bound of cost ratio. Combining the two lemmas gives

A⁡(In,q(h))OPT​(In,q(h))≥n⁡(n+q)12​(n2+n+q2+q)+h​q.{}\frac{A(I^{(h)}_{n,q})}{\textnormal{{OPT}}(I^{(h)}_{n,q})}\geq\frac{n(n+q)}{\tfrac{1}{2}(n^{2}+n+q^{2}+q)+hq}\ . (18)

The parameter qq controls the tradeoff. Each extra request adds nn to the online cost, while the part of the offline bound that depends on qq is q⁡(q+1)2+h​q\frac{q(q+1)}{2}+hq. Thus increasing qq raises the online cost linearly but the offline bound quadratically.

Proof of Theorem 3.10.

To choose qq, we first maximize the right-hand side of Equation 18 over real values of qq. Differentiating with respect to qq gives the maximizer

q∗=2​n​(n−h)−n.q^{*}=\sqrt{2n(n-h)}-n.

Since qq must be a positive integer, we set

q=max⁡{1,⌊q∗⌋}.q=\max\{1,\lfloor q^{*}\rfloor\}.

Because 0<q∗<n/2<n−h0<q^{*}<n/2<n-h, this choice satisfies 1≤q≤n−h1\leq q\leq n-h and |q−q∗|≤1|q-q^{*}|\leq 1.

By the two lemmas, the reciprocal of the actual cost ratio is at most

OPT​(In,q(h))A⁡(In,q(h))\displaystyle\frac{\textnormal{{OPT}}(I^{(h)}_{n,q})}{A(I^{(h)}_{n,q})} ≤12​(n2+n+q2+q)+h​qn⁡(n+q)\displaystyle\leq\frac{\tfrac{1}{2}(n^{2}+n+q^{2}+q)+hq}{n(n+q)}
=q∗+hn+(q−q∗)22​n​(n+q)+12​n\displaystyle=\frac{q^{*}+h}{n}+\frac{(q-q^{*})^{2}}{2n(n+q)}+\frac{1}{2n}
≤q∗+h+1n.\displaystyle\leq\frac{q^{*}+h+1}{n}.

The equality uses (q∗)2+2​n​q∗=n2−2​n​h(q^{*})^{2}+2nq^{*}=n^{2}-2nh. Taking reciprocals and substituting q∗q^{*} proves the desired bound. ∎

Note that for algorithms that permit no early services (h=0h=0), the bound with h=1h=1 applies, since every such algorithm is also 11-local-lazy MTF.

Lemma A.3.

FER is 11-local-lazy MTF.

Proof.

By definition, FER uses no paid swaps, moves each accessed element to the front, and serves early only at the head. ∎

Corollary A.4.

Over all list sizes, the worst-case cost ratio of FER is at least 1+21+\sqrt{2}, even on inputs without self-overlap.

Proof.

By Lemma A.3, apply Theorem 3.10 with h=1h=1. For every n≥3n\geq 3, this gives an input with

FER​(σ)OPT​(σ)≥12−2/n−1+2/n≥12−1+2/n.\frac{\textnormal{{FER}}(\sigma)}{\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma)}\geq\frac{1}{\sqrt{2-2/n}-1+2/n}\geq\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}-1+2/n}.

For any 0<c<1+20<c<1+\sqrt{2}, choose an integer n≥3n\geq 3 with

n>21/c−(2−1).n>\frac{2}{1/c-(\sqrt{2}-1)}.

The resulting ratio exceeds cc. A nonpositive cc fails on every nonempty input. ∎

Remark A.5.

The construction above establishes a lower bound for guarantees of the form A⁡(σ)≤c​OPT​(σ)A(\sigma)\leq c\,\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma), without an additive term. It does not by itself establish the same lower bound when the guarantee allows

A⁡(σ)≤c​OPT​(σ)+β⁡(n),A(\sigma)\leq c\,\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma)+\beta(n),

where β⁡(n)\beta(n) may depend on the list size but not on the number of requests. Indeed, our instance has only n+q≤2​nn+q\leq 2n requests and online cost at most 2​n22n^{2}, so an allowance of β⁡(n)=2​n2\beta(n)=2n^{2} would cover its entire online cost.

To rule out such a guarantee, we would need inputs on a fixed number of elements for which A⁡(σ)−c​OPT​(σ)A(\sigma)-c\,\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma) grows without bound. This requires an additional construction or repetition argument. Letting nn grow in the present construction is insufficient, since β⁡(n)\beta(n) may grow with it.

A.3 The FER-specific lower bound

In this subsection, we prove a finite-nn lower bound and use it to prove Theorem 3.11.

Lemma A.6.

Fix n≥2n\geq 2. If FER​(σ)≤c​OPT​(σ)+β⁡(n)\textnormal{{FER}}(\sigma)\leq c\,\textnormal{{OPT}}(\sigma)+\beta(n) for every input σ\sigma on an nn-element list, then

c≥3​n2n2+5​n−3.c\geq\frac{3n^{2}}{n^{2}+5n-3}.
Proof.

Construction. Let the initial list be (en,…,e1)(e_{n},\ldots,e_{1}). Requests are released in the repeating order

e1,…,en,e1,…,en,…,e_{1},\ldots,e_{n},\quad e_{1},\ldots,e_{n},\quad\ldots,

with release time and deadline

ri=2​i+3,di=2​n+2​ir_{i}=2i+3,\qquad d_{i}=2n+2i

for the iith request. We check that each window has length 2​n−3≥12n-3\geq 1. Also, requests to the same element do not overlap, since ri+n=di+3r_{i+n}=d_{i}+3.

We organize the input into groups of 3​n3n requests, each group consisting of three repetitions of requests for e1,⋯,ene_{1},\cdots,e_{n}. We analyze the per group cost for FER and our offline schedule.

Online cost of FER. We show that FER costs 3​n23n^{2} per group. FER serves requests early only through head clearance at a deadline. We first show that this never happens by induction.

At the first deadline d1=2​n+2d_{1}=2n+2, the head is ene_{n}, and the first request for ene_{n} arrives at rn=2​n+3r_{n}=2n+3, so head clearance does nothing and FER serves request 11 at its deadline.

Now suppose FER has served requests 1,…,i1,\ldots,i, each at its deadline. The element e^i\hat{e}_{i} requested by request ii is at the front. The next request for e^i\hat{e}_{i}, if present, arrives at ri+n=di+3r_{i+n}=d_{i}+3, whereas the next deadline is di+1=di+2d_{i+1}=d_{i}+2. Thus the next deadline arrives before the head e^i\hat{e}_{i}’s next request. Since FER makes no moves between deadlines, nothing happens until FER serves request i+1i+1 at its deadline. By induction, every request is served at its deadline.

These accesses visit the elements in reverse initial order, so each requested element is always positioned last in the list. Each repetition restores the initial list. Hence every access costs nn, and every group of three repetitions costs 3​n23n^{2}.

Cheaper offline scheme. Consider an offline schedule that uses the first repetition to arrange the list in ascending order, and then serve the requests in the second repetition at deadlines and the requests in the third at release, reducing the costs of access in both repetitions.

More specifically, consider three consecutive repetitions, starting with the reversed list (en,…,e1)(e_{n},\ldots,e_{1}), and let DD be deadline of the request to e1e_{1} in the first repetition of the current group. We describe the schedule relative to this deadline.

  1. 1.

    First repetition: arrange the list using free move to front. Observe that the request to ene_{n} in the first repetition of the group arrives at D+1D+1, while all other requests in the first repetition have arrived by D−1D-1.

    At time DD, serve in this order en−1,en−2,…,e1,e_{n-1},e_{n-2},\ldots,e_{1}, moving each element to the front for free after serving it. These requests all have deadlines at least DD, so the services are feasible. Their access positions are 2,3,…,n2,3,\ldots,n, and the resulting list is (e1,e2,…,en).(e_{1},e_{2},\ldots,e_{n}). At time D+1D+1, serve the newly released request to ene_{n} at position nn, without moving it. The first repetition is now complete, and the list remains ascending. The total cost of this repetition is

    ∑j=2nj+n=n⁡(n+1)2+n−1.\sum_{j=2}^{n}j+n=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}+n-1.
  2. 2.

    Second repetition: serve requests at deadlines. Serve each request in the second repetition at its deadline and move its element to the front. The access to eje_{j} costs jj: before this access, all earlier services in the second and third repetitions only rearrange smaller-index elements, which were already ahead of eje_{j}. Thus the second repetition costs

    ∑j=1nj=n⁡(n+1)2.\sum_{j=1}^{n}j=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}.
  3. 3.

    Third repetition: serve requests at release. Serve each request in the third repetition as soon as it arrives and move its element to the front.

    If eje_{j} receives its second service at time tt, its third service is at t+3t+3, by rj+n=dj+3r_{j+n}=d_{j}+3. Immediately after its second service, eje_{j} is at the front. Between the second and third service of eje_{j}, only two elements can move ahead of it: ej−1e_{j-1} through its third service at t+1t+1 (if j>1j>1), and ej+1e_{j+1} through its second service at t+2t+2 (if j<nj<n). There are no other intervening services, since services within either of these repetitions are two time units apart. Therefore the first and last accesses in the third repetition cost 22 each, and the other n−2n-2 accesses cost 33 each. The total is

    2+3​(n−2)+2=3​n−2.2+3(n-2)+2=3n-2.

Finally, adding the costs of the three repetitions gives a cost per group of

(n⁡(n+1)2+n−1)+n⁡(n+1)2+(3​n−2)=n2+5​n−3.\left(\frac{n(n+1)}{2}+n-1\right)+\frac{n(n+1)}{2}+(3n-2)=n^{2}+5n-3.

Each element’s last access serves its request in the third repetition. These services occur in order e1,…,ene_{1},\ldots,e_{n}, leaving the list reversed again. The last such service occurs at the last release of the request for ene_{n} in the third repetition at time D+4​n+1D+4n+1; the next group’s first request arrives at D+4​n+3D+4n+3. Thus all requests in these three repetitions are served and the initial list order of (en,⋯,e1)(e_{n},\cdots,e_{1}) is restored before the next group begins arriving. We can repeat the schedule directly, stopping after any complete group.

Fix nn and use arbitrarily many groups of three repetitions. Each group adds cost 3​n23n^{2} to FER and n2+5​n−3n^{2}+5n-3 to the offline schedule. The fixed additive allowance β⁡(n)\beta(n) becomes negligible per group, so any competitive guarantee requires 3​n2≤c⁡(n2+5​n−3)3n^{2}\leq c(n^{2}+5n-3), hence

c≥3​n2n2+5​n−3.c\geq\frac{3n^{2}}{n^{2}+5n-3}.

∎

Proof of Theorem 3.11.

The upper bound follows from Theorem 3.2. For the lower bound, Lemma A.6 gives

c≥3​n2n2+5​n−3.c\geq\frac{3n^{2}}{n^{2}+5n-3}.

Letting n→∞n\to\infty shows that no uniform competitive constant below 33 is possible. ∎
